title: Yarn over as an increase
subtitle: The increase that also opens an eyelet.
excerpt: A yarn over (abbreviated yo) wraps the working yarn around the needle to create a new loop, increasing the stitch count by one and leaving a small eyelet. It is both the standard lace increase and the building block of eyelet patterns.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), lace chapter. Weldon's Practical Knitter lace series (1888 onward). Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870).

glossaryTerms.definition: A motion that wraps the working yarn over the right needle to create a new loop. When worked on the next row, this loop becomes a stitch, increasing the stitch count by one. It also creates a small eyelet in the fabric. Abbreviated yo. UK patterns may write yfwd (yarn forward), yrn (yarn round needle), or yo depending on the context.
A small decorative hole in knitted fabric, created by working a yarn over followed by a decrease (or by working a yarn over without a compensating decrease as a deliberate increase).

content.text: (abbreviated yo; older UK patterns use yfwd for 'yarn forward' between two knit stitches) wraps the working yarn around the right needle once. When the next row reaches this loop, it is knitted or purled like any other stitch, adding one to the stitch count. In lace, a yo is always paired with a decrease so the count stays level, and the two together form one of the
in the lace pattern. When used without a paired decrease, it is a plain increase. Difficulty: beginner.
After completing a knit stitch, the yarn sits at the back of the work.
Bring the yarn forward between the needles to the front.
Take the yarn back over the top of the right needle to the back again, ready to knit the next stitch.
Knit the next stitch. The yarn over now sits as a loop on the right needle, one stitch added.

Between a knit and a purl (yon, yarn over needle): after the knit stitch, bring the yarn forward and take it all the way around the right needle before purling. The loop will sit correctly for the purl stitch.

Every lace pattern uses yarn overs paired with decreases as its basic unit. Raglan shawls and top-down yokes use yarn overs for their decorative increase lines. Simple eyelet patterns for baby blankets often use a yarn over and k2tog in alternating positions to create an allover spot pattern. The yarn over is also the starting action for the yarn over in the German twisted cast-on.

items.symptom: The eyelet does not appear on the right side
items.cause: Yarn over worked as a purl bump rather than an open loop on the next row
items.fix: On the following row, the yarn-over loop should sit with its leading leg on the front of the needle. Knit into the front of it; do not twist it by knitting into the back.

items.symptom: Stitch count grows unexpectedly from beginning of row
items.cause: The yarn at the start of a purl row was at the back rather than the front, and was taken over the needle before the first purl
items.fix: Confirm yarn position before the first stitch of every row. If the first stitch is a purl, the yarn should already be at the front.

items.symptom: Hole is too large or too small compared to the pattern example
items.cause: Working too loosely or too tightly
items.fix: The hole size is largely governed by the needle size. Blocking opens up the eyelet; a tighter yarn-over simply closes it slightly on the needle.
